nodes.name: Coloring
nodes.statement: Given a set of objects $X$ and a set of colors $Y$, we interpret functions in $Y^X = \{f : X \to Y\}$ as \emph{colorings} of $X$ with colors in $Y$.

nodes.name: Group action
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group. A (left) \emph{group action} of $G$ on a set $X$ is a function ${-} \cdot {-} : G \times X \to X$ that satisfies: \begin{align*} 1 \cdot x &= x \quad \forall x \in X,\\ g \cdot (h \cdot x) &= (gh) \cdot x \quad \forall g, h \in G, \forall x \in X. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A left group action is a map $G\times X\to X$ with $1\cdot x=x$ and $g\cdot(h\cdot x)=(gh)\cdot x$.

nodes.name: Quotient set X/G
nodes.statement: A group action induces an equivalence relation on $X$ defined by \begin{equation*} x \sim y \iff \exists g \in G : g \cdot x = y. \end{equation*} The quotient set $X / G$ is the set of equivalence classes under this relation.
nodes.statement_short: Orbit relation $x\sim y$ iff $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g$; $X/G$ is its set of classes.

nodes.name: Orbit
nodes.statement: The equivalence class of an element $x \in X$ is called the \emph{orbit of $x$} and is denoted as $Gx = \{g \cdot x : g \in G\}$.

nodes.name: Fixed points
nodes.statement: The set of \emph{fixed points} of $g \in G$ is $X^g = \{x \in X : g \cdot x = x\}$.

nodes.name: Stabilizer
nodes.statement: The \emph{stabilizer} of $x \in X$ is $G_x = \{g \in G : g \cdot x = x\}$.

nodes.name: Equivalent colorings
nodes.statement: Thus, for any $g \in G$, we consider the colorings $f$ and $x \mapsto f(g^{-1} \cdot x)$ to be equivalent.

nodes.name: Induced group action on colorings
nodes.statement: Given a group action of $G$ on $X$, we can define an induced group action of $G$ on $Y^X$ by: \begin{equation*} g \cdot f = \big(x \mapsto f(g^{-1} \cdot x)\big). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Given a group action of $G$ on $X$
conclusions: we can define an induced group action of $G$ on $Y^X$ by: \begin{equation*} g \cdot f = \big(x \mapsto f(g^{-1} \cdot x)\big). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: An action of $G$ on $X$ induces an action on colorings by $(g\cdot f)(x)=f(g^{-1}\cdot x)$.
nodes.label: prop:MulActionColorings

nodes.name: Proof of Induced group action on colorings
nodes.statement: \begin{gather*} (1 \cdot f)(x) = f(1^{-1} \cdot x) = f(1 \cdot x) = f(x), \\ (g \cdot (h \cdot f))(x) = f(h^{-1} \cdot (g^{-1} \cdot x)) = f((h^{-1}g^{-1}) \cdot x) = f((gh)^{-1} \cdot x) = ((gh) \cdot f)(x). \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct verification of the two group-action axioms.

nodes.name: Finiteness of the set of orbits of colorings
nodes.statement: When $X$ and $Y$ are finite, the set of orbits $Y^X/G$ is also finite.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are finite
conclusions: the set of orbits $Y^X/G$ is also finite

nodes.name: Finiteness of X and Y
nodes.statement: From this point onward, we will assume that both $X$ and $Y$ are finite.

nodes.name: Number of distinct colorings
nodes.statement: The \emph{number of distinct colorings} is defined as $|Y^X/G|$.
nodes.label: def:numDistinctColorings

nodes.name: Symmetric group S_X
nodes.statement: A group action of $G$ on $X$ associates each element $g \in G$ with a permutation in $S_X = \{\pi : X \to X \mid \pi \text{ is bijective}\}$.
nodes.section: 2 Cycles of elements in a group

nodes.name: Permutation pi_g
nodes.statement: Specifically, each $g \in G$ is mapped to a permutation $\pi_g$ defined by $\pi_g(x) = g \cdot x$.
nodes.section: 2 Cycles of elements in a group

nodes.name: Action homomorphism into S_X
nodes.statement: The mapping $\phi : G \to S_X$, given by $\phi(g) = \pi_g$, is a group homomorphism.
nodes.section: 2 Cycles of elements in a group
assumptions: The mapping $\phi : G \to S_X$, given by $\phi(g) = \pi_g$
conclusions: is a group homomorphism

nodes.name: Cycles of a group element
nodes.statement: Given $g \in G$, the set of \emph{cycles of $g$} is defined as $X / \sim_g$, where $\sim_g$ is the equivalence relation of being in the same cycle of $g$: \begin{equation*} x_1 \sim_g x_2 \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{Z}: \pi_g^k(x_1) = x_2. \end{equation*} The \emph{number of cycles of $g$} is: $c(g) = |X / \sim_g|$.\\ The \emph{number of elements in $G$ with exactly $i$ cycles} is: $|\{g \in G \mid c(g) = i\}|$.
nodes.section: 2 Cycles of elements in a group
definiendum: number of elements in $G$ with exactly $i$ cycles
also_stated_at: Using this correspondence, we define the \emph{cycles of $g$} as the cycles of the permutation $\pi_g$.
The number of cycles of $g$ is denoted by $c(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: Cycles of $g$ are classes of $x_1\sim_g x_2$ iff $\pi_g^k(x_1)=x_2$; $c(g)$ counts them.
nodes.label: def:CyclesOfGroup

nodes.name: Colorings of cycles
nodes.statement: Colorings of the cycles of $g \in G$ are then defined as functions in $Y^{X / \sim_g}$.
nodes.section: 2 Cycles of elements in a group

nodes.name: Burnside's lemma
nodes.statement: Mathlib already includes an important result known as \emph{Burnside's lemma}, which states that for any finite group $G$ acting on a set $X$, the number of orbits is equal to the average number of fixed points: \begin{equation*} |X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |X^g|. \end{equation*}
also_stated_at: This is formalized in Mathlib as \emph{MulAction.sum\_card\_fixedBy\_eq\_card\_orbits\_mul\_card\_group}: \begin{equation*} |X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{g \in G} |X^g|. \end{equation*}
assumptions: for any finite group $G$ acting on a set $X$
conclusions: the number of orbits is equal to the average number of fixed points
nodes.statement_short: The number of orbits equals the average number of fixed points.

nodes.name: Fixed colorings are constant on cycles
nodes.statement: For any $g \in G$: \begin{equation*} f \in (Y^X)^g \iff \forall x_1, x_2 \in X: (x_1 \sim_g x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2)). \end{equation*}
also_stated_at: First, we prove that for any $g \in G$, a coloring $f$ is a fixed point of $g$ if and only if $f$ maps all elements in the same cycle of $g$ to the same color.
assumptions: For any $g \in G$
conclusions: f \in (Y^X)^g \iff \forall x_1, x_2 \in X: (x_1 \sim_g x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2)).
equivalent_conditions: \forall x_1, x_2 \in X: (x_1 \sim_g x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2))
nodes.statement_short: A coloring is fixed by $g$ iff it is constant on each cycle of $g$.
nodes.label: prop:f-mem-fixedBy-iff-forall-eq-to-eq

nodes.name: Proof of Fixed colorings are constant on cycles
nodes.statement: \begin{align} f \in (Y^X)^g &\iff g \cdot f = f, \\ &\iff \forall x \in X: (g \cdot f)(x) = f(x), \\ &\iff \forall x \in X: f(g^{-1} \cdot x) = f(x), \\ &\iff \forall x \in X, \forall k \in \mathbb{Z}: f(g^k \cdot x) = f(x), \\ &\iff \forall x_1, x_2 \in X: (x_1 \sim_g x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2)). \end{align} The $(3) \implies (4)$ implication is proven inductively.\\ If $k = 0$ then $f(1 \cdot x) = f(x)$ by the first property of group action.\\ If $k \geq 1$ then we use (3) on $g^{k} \cdot x$ to get $f(g^{k - 1} \cdot x) = f(g^k \cdot x)$ and then use the induction hypothesis $f(g^{k - 1} \cdot x) = f(x)$ to conclude $f(g^k \cdot x) = f(x)$.\\ If $k \leq -1$ then we use (3) on $g^{k + 1} \cdot x$ to get $f(g^k \cdot x) = f(g^{k + 1} \cdot x)$ and then use the induction hypothesis $f(g^{k + 1} \cdot x) = f(x)$ to conclude $f(g^k \cdot x) = f(x)$.\\ \\ To prove that $(4) \iff (5)$ we use the fact that $x_1 \sim_g x_2 \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{Z}: g^k \cdot x_1 = x_2$.\\ The $(4) \implies (5)$ implication follows by using $(4)$ with $x = x_1$ and $k$ from $\exists k \in \mathbb{Z}: g^k \cdot x_1 = x_2$.\\ The $(5) \implies (4)$ implication follows by using $(5)$ with $x_1 = g^k \cdot x$ and $x_2 = x$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of equivalences; the step (3)$\Rightarrow$(4) by induction on $k$ in both directions.

nodes.name: Chain of equivalences for fixed colorings
nodes.statement: f \in (Y^X)^g &\iff g \cdot f = f, \\ &\iff \forall x \in X: (g \cdot f)(x) = f(x), \\ &\iff \forall x \in X: f(g^{-1} \cdot x) = f(x), \\ &\iff \forall x \in X, \forall k \in \mathbb{Z}: f(g^k \cdot x) = f(x), \\ &\iff \forall x_1, x_2 \in X: (x_1 \sim_g x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2)).
nodes.statement_short: Fixed coloring iff invariant under $g^{-1}$, iff under all $g^k$, iff constant on cycles.

nodes.name: Bijection between fixed colorings and colorings of cycles
nodes.statement: Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$ in $X/\sim_g$.\\ Let $\varphi : (Y^X)^g \to Y^{X/\sim_g}$ be defined by $\varphi(f) = ([x] \mapsto f(x'))$, where $x'$ is some element of $[x]$.\\ Let $\varphi^{-1} : Y^{X/\sim_g} \to (Y^X)^g$ be defined by $\varphi^{-1}(f) = (x \mapsto f([x]))$.\\ Then $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are well-defined and mutually inverse. Therefore we have a bijection between $(Y^X)^g$ and $Y^{X/\sim_g}$.
assumptions: Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$ in $X/\sim_g$.
Let $\varphi : (Y^X)^g \to Y^{X/\sim_g}$ be defined by $\varphi(f) = ([x] \mapsto f(x'))$, where $x'$ is some element of $[x]$.
Let $\varphi^{-1} : Y^{X/\sim_g} \to (Y^X)^g$ be defined by $\varphi^{-1}(f) = (x \mapsto f([x]))$.
conclusions: Then $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are well-defined and mutually inverse.
Therefore we have a bijection between $(Y^X)^g$ and $Y^{X/\sim_g}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed colorings of $g$ are in bijection with colorings of the cycles of $g$.
nodes.label: prop:equiv-of-fixedBy-coloring-of-cycle-coloring

nodes.name: Proof of Bijection between fixed colorings and colorings of cycles
nodes.statement: $\varphi$ is well-defined because, by Proposition~\ref{prop:f-mem-fixedBy-iff-forall-eq-to-eq}, $f \in (Y^X)^g$ and $x_1 \sim_g x_2$ imply $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$.\\ $\varphi^{-1}$ is well-defined because it maps to $(Y^X)^g$: \begin{equation*} \forall f \in Y^{X/\sim_g}, \forall x \in X: (g \cdot \varphi^{-1}(f))(x) = f([g^{-1} \cdot x]) = f([x]) = (\varphi^{-1}(f))(x). \end{equation*} $\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(f))(x) = f(x')$, where $x'$ is some representative of $[x]$. Therefore we have $x \sim_g x'$ and since $f \in (Y^X)^g$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:f-mem-fixedBy-iff-forall-eq-to-eq}: $f(x) = f(x')$.\\ $\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(f))([x]) = f([x'])$ where $x'$ is some representative of $[x]$. Since $[x] = [x']$, it follows that $f([x]) = f([x'])$.
nodes.statement_short: Check well-definedness of both maps and that they are mutually inverse.

nodes.name: Well-definedness of $\varphi$ from Proposition 2
nodes.statement: $\varphi$ is well-defined because, by Proposition~\ref{prop:f-mem-fixedBy-iff-forall-eq-to-eq}, $f \in (Y^X)^g$ and $x_1 \sim_g x_2$ imply $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness of $\varphi$ from Proposition 2

nodes.name: Well-definedness of $\varphi^{-1}$ by direct computation
nodes.statement: $\varphi^{-1}$ is well-defined because it maps to $(Y^X)^g$: \begin{equation*} \forall f \in Y^{X/\sim_g}, \forall x \in X: (g \cdot \varphi^{-1}(f))(x) = f([g^{-1} \cdot x]) = f([x]) = (\varphi^{-1}(f))(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness of $\varphi^{-1}$ by direct computation

nodes.name: Left inverse via Proposition 2
nodes.statement: $\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(f))(x) = f(x')$, where $x'$ is some representative of $[x]$. Therefore we have $x \sim_g x'$ and since $f \in (Y^X)^g$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:f-mem-fixedBy-iff-forall-eq-to-eq}: $f(x) = f(x')$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Left inverse via Proposition 2

nodes.name: Right inverse since $[x]=[x']$
nodes.statement: $\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(f))([x]) = f([x'])$ where $x'$ is some representative of $[x]$. Since $[x] = [x']$, it follows that $f([x]) = f([x'])$.
nodes.statement_short: Right inverse since $[x]=[x']$

nodes.name: Number of fixed colorings equals |Y|^c(g)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \forall g \in G: |(Y^X)^g| = |Y|^{c(g)} \end{equation*}
assumptions: \forall g \in G
nodes.statement_short: Each $g$ fixes exactly $|Y|^{c(g)}$ colorings.
nodes.label: prop:forall-card-pow-numCyclesOfGroup-eq-card-fixedBy

nodes.name: Proof of Number of fixed colorings equals |Y|^c(g)
nodes.statement: The equality $|(Y^X)^g| = |Y^{X/\sim_g}|$ follows from the bijection in Proposition~\ref{prop:equiv-of-fixedBy-coloring-of-cycle-coloring}. The number of functions in $Y^{X/\sim_g}$ is $|Y|^{|X/\sim_g|}$. By definition, $c(g) = |X/\sim_g|$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Count via the bijection of Proposition 3 and $|Y^{X/\sim_g}|=|Y|^{c(g)}$.

nodes.name: Transfer cardinality via the bijection
nodes.statement: The equality $|(Y^X)^g| = |Y^{X/\sim_g}|$ follows from the bijection in Proposition~\ref{prop:equiv-of-fixedBy-coloring-of-cycle-coloring}.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer cardinality via the bijection

nodes.name: Count functions on the quotient
nodes.statement: The number of functions in $Y^{X/\sim_g}$ is $|Y|^{|X/\sim_g|}$.
nodes.statement_short: Count functions on the quotient

nodes.name: Rewrite by the definition of $c(g)$
nodes.statement: By definition, $c(g) = |X/\sim_g|$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite by the definition of $c(g)$

nodes.name: Pólya's enumeration theorem
nodes.statement: \emph{(Pólya's enumeration theorem)} The number of distinct colorings of $X$ with colors in $Y$ under the group action of $G$ on $X$ is: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{c(g)}. \end{equation*} A version of the theorem that preserves the fact that $\sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{c(g)}$ is divisible by $|G|$ is also provided: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{c(g)}. \end{equation*}
assumptions: under the group action of $G$ on $X$
conclusions: |Y^X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{c(g)}.
|Y^X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{c(g)}.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct colorings equal the average over $G$ of $|Y|^{c(g)}$; also in division-free form.
nodes.label: prop:numDistinctColorings-eq-sum-card-pow-numCyclesOfGroup-div-mul-card-group

nodes.name: Proof of Pólya's enumeration theorem
nodes.statement: We use \emph{Burnside's lemma} on colorings to get: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{g \in G} |(Y^X)^g|. \end{equation*} Using Proposition~\ref{prop:forall-card-pow-numCyclesOfGroup-eq-card-fixedBy}, we substitute $|(Y^X)^g|$ with $|Y|^{c(g)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Burnside's lemma on colorings, then substitute the fixed-point count of Proposition 4.

nodes.name: Pólya's enumeration theorem (sum over numbers of cycles)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{i \in [|X| + 1]} |\{g \in G \mid c(g) = i\}| \cdot |Y|^i. \end{equation*}
conclusions: |Y^X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{i \in [|X| + 1]} |\{g \in G \mid c(g) = i\}| \cdot |Y|^i.
nodes.statement_short: Pólya's formula regrouped by the number of cycles $i$ of group elements.
nodes.label: prop:numDistinctColorings-mul-card-group-eq-sum-numGroupOfNumCycles-mul-card-pow

nodes.name: Proof of Pólya's enumeration theorem (sum over numbers of cycles)
nodes.statement: For any $g \in G$ we have $0 \leq c(g) \leq |X|$. Then: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| \cdot |G| = \sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{c(g)} = \sum_{i \in [|X| + 1]} \sum_{g' \in \{g \in G \mid c(g) = i\}} |Y|^i = \sum_{i \in [|X| + 1]} |\{g \in G \mid c(g) = i\}| \cdot |Y|^i. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Regroup the Pólya sum by the value of $c(g)\in[0,|X|]$.

nodes.name: Cycles of a permutation
nodes.statement: Given a permutation $\pi \in S_X$, the set of \emph{cycles of $\pi$} is defined as $X / \sim_\pi$, where $\sim_\pi$ is the equivalence relation of being in the same cycle of $\pi$: \begin{equation*} x_1 \sim_\pi x_2 \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{Z}: \pi^k(x_1) = x_2. \end{equation*} The \emph{number of cycles of $\pi$} is: \begin{equation*} c(\pi) = |X / \sim_\pi|. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Cycles of $\pi$ are classes of $x_1\sim_\pi x_2$ iff $\pi^k(x_1)=x_2$; $c(\pi)$ counts them.
nodes.label: def:numCyclesOfPerm

nodes.name: Number of cycles equals size of a set of representatives
nodes.statement: For a permutation $\pi \in S_X$ and a set $S$ containing exactly one element from each cycle of $\pi$, we have $c(\pi) = |S|$.
assumptions: a permutation $\pi \in S_X$
a set $S$ containing exactly one element from each cycle of $\pi$
nodes.label: prop:numCyclesOfPerm-eq-card

nodes.name: Proof of Number of cycles equals size of a set of representatives
nodes.statement: We construct a bijection $\varphi : X / \sim_\pi \to S$ defined by: \begin{align*} \varphi([x]) &= \text{the unique element in } S \text{ that lies in the same cycle as } x,\\ \varphi^{-1}(x) &= [x]. \end{align*} Since $\varphi$ is a bijection, we conclude that $c(\pi) = |S|$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct a bijection between the cycles and the representatives.

nodes.name: Every point returns under some power of a permutation
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be a permutation on a finite set $X$, and $x \in X$. Then there exists some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that: \begin{equation*} \pi^{n + 1}(x) = x. \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $\pi$ be a permutation on a finite set $X$, and $x \in X$.
conclusions: there exists some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that: \begin{equation*} \pi^{n + 1}(x) = x. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: prop:exists-perm-pow

nodes.name: Proof of Every point returns under some power of a permutation
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is finite, the cycle containing $x$ has finite length. We set $n$ to be the length of this cycle minus $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $n$ to be the length of the cycle of $x$ minus one.

nodes.name: Reduction of permutation powers
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $\pi^n(x) = x$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for any $m, r \in \mathbb{N}$, we have: \begin{equation*} \pi^{m \cdot n + r}(x) = \pi^r(x). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $\pi^n(x) = x$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: \pi^{m \cdot n + r}(x) = \pi^r(x).
nodes.label: prop:perm-pow-reduce

nodes.name: Proof of Reduction of permutation powers
nodes.statement: We prove this by induction on $m$.\\ If $m = 0$, the equation follows immediately.\\ If $m > 0$, then \begin{equation*} \pi^{(m + 1) \cdot n + r}(x) = \pi^{m \cdot n + r}(\pi^n(x)) = \pi^{m \cdot n + r}(x), \end{equation*} and we can use the inductive hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $m$.

nodes.name: Integer powers reduce to powers below the period
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $\pi^{n + 1}(x) = x$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for any $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ there exists an $m \in [n + 1]$ such that: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = \pi^m(x). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $\pi$ be a permutation such that $\pi^{n + 1}(x) = x$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: for any $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ there exists an $m \in [n + 1]$ such that: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = \pi^m(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: prop:forall-exists-lt-perm-pow-eq-perm-pow

nodes.name: Proof of Integer powers reduce to powers below the period
nodes.statement: We use $m = k \bmod (n + 1)$. We will apply Proposition~\ref{prop:perm-pow-reduce}, which requires natural numbers, so we split the proof into cases based on whether $k \geq 0$.\\ If $k \geq 0$, we have: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = \pi^{\lfloor \frac{k}{n + 1}\rfloor \cdot (n + 1) + (k \bmod (n + 1))}(x) = \pi^m(x). \end{equation*} If $k < 0$, we have: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{-k}(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{\lfloor \frac{-k}{n + 1}\rfloor \cdot (n + 1) + (-k \bmod (n + 1))}(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{-k \bmod (n + 1)}(x) = \pi^{-(-k \bmod (n + 1))}(x). \end{equation*} If $k \bmod (n + 1) = 0$, this is equal to $\pi^m(x)$.\\ Otherwise, we use $\pi^{n + 1}(x) = x$ to increment the power by $n + 1$, making the expression equal to: \begin{equation*} \pi^{n + 1 - (n + 1 - (k \bmod (n + 1)))}(x) = \pi^m(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Take $m=k \bmod (n+1)$ and split on the sign of $k$, applying Proposition 7.

nodes.name: Choose $m=k\bmod(n+1)$ and split on the sign of $k$
nodes.statement: We use $m = k \bmod (n + 1)$. We will apply Proposition~\ref{prop:perm-pow-reduce}, which requires natural numbers, so we split the proof into cases based on whether $k \geq 0$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Choose $m=k\bmod(n+1)$ and split on the sign of $k$

nodes.name: Case $k\ge 0$ via Proposition 7
nodes.statement: If $k \geq 0$, we have: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = \pi^{\lfloor \frac{k}{n + 1}\rfloor \cdot (n + 1) + (k \bmod (n + 1))}(x) = \pi^m(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Case $k\ge 0$ via Proposition 7

nodes.name: Case $k<0$ via $\pi^{-1}$
nodes.statement: If $k < 0$, we have: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{-k}(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{\lfloor \frac{-k}{n + 1}\rfloor \cdot (n + 1) + (-k \bmod (n + 1))}(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{-k \bmod (n + 1)}(x) = \pi^{-(-k \bmod (n + 1))}(x). \end{equation*} If $k \bmod (n + 1) = 0$, this is equal to $\pi^m(x)$.\\ Otherwise, we use $\pi^{n + 1}(x) = x$ to increment the power by $n + 1$, making the expression equal to: \begin{equation*} \pi^{n + 1 - (n + 1 - (k \bmod (n + 1)))}(x) = \pi^m(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Case $k<0$ via $\pi^{-1}$

nodes.name: Rewrite with $\pi^{-1}$ and reduce
nodes.statement: If $k < 0$, we have: \begin{equation*} \pi^k(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{-k}(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{\lfloor \frac{-k}{n + 1}\rfloor \cdot (n + 1) + (-k \bmod (n + 1))}(x) = (\pi^{-1})^{-k \bmod (n + 1)}(x) = \pi^{-(-k \bmod (n + 1))}(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite with $\pi^{-1}$ and reduce

nodes.statement: We define the bijection: \begin{equation*} \varphi : Y^X/G \to Y^{[|X|]}/G, \quad [f] \mapsto [f \circ \phi^{-1}] \end{equation*} with inverse \begin{equation*} \varphi^{-1} : Y^{[|X|]}/G \to Y^X/G, \quad [f] \mapsto [f \circ \phi]. \end{equation*} These are well-defined, since for any $f, h \in Y^X$ with $f = g \cdot h$, we have: \begin{align*} (f \circ \phi^{-1}) &= (g \cdot h) \circ \phi^{-1} \\ &= (x \mapsto h(g^{-1} \cdot x)) \circ \phi^{-1} \\ &= i \mapsto h(g^{-1} \cdot \phi^{-1}(i)) \\ &= i \mapsto h(\phi^{-1}(\phi(g^{-1} \cdot \phi^{-1}(i)))) \\ &= i \mapsto ((h \circ \phi^{-1})(g^{-1} \cdot i)) \\ &= g \cdot (h \circ \phi^{-1}). \end{align*} and similarly, for any $f, h \in Y^{[|X|]}$ such that $f = g \cdot h$, we have: \begin{equation*} f \circ \phi = g \cdot (h \circ \phi). \end{equation*} Since $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are mutually inverse, it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| = |Y^{[|X|]}/G|. \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: These are well-defined, since for any $f, h \in Y^X$ with $f = g \cdot h$, we have: \begin{align*} (f \circ \phi^{-1}) &= (g \cdot h) \circ \phi^{-1} \\ &= (x \mapsto h(g^{-1} \cdot x)) \circ \phi^{-1} \\ &= i \mapsto h(g^{-1} \cdot \phi^{-1}(i)) \\ &= i \mapsto h(\phi^{-1}(\phi(g^{-1} \cdot \phi^{-1}(i)))) \\ &= i \mapsto ((h \circ \phi^{-1})(g^{-1} \cdot i)) \\ &= g \cdot (h \circ \phi^{-1}). \end{align*} and similarly, for any $f, h \in Y^{[|X|]}$ such that $f = g \cdot h$, we have: \begin{equation*} f \circ \phi = g \cdot (h \circ \phi). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Both maps respect the group action

nodes.name: Equal cardinalities

nodes.name: Correctness of computeNumDistinctColorings
nodes.statement: The function \emph{computeNumDistinctColorings} computes the number of distinct colorings of $X$ with colors in $Y$ under the group action of $G$. It uses \emph{Pólya's enumeration theorem} and the function \emph{computeNumCyclesOfPerm} to count cycles of permutations: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |Y|^{\textit{computeNumCyclesOfPerm} (\phi \circ \pi_g \circ \phi^{-1})}. \end{equation*}
conclusions: The function \emph{computeNumDistinctColorings} computes the number of distinct colorings of $X$ with colors in $Y$ under the group action of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: computeNumDistinctColorings evaluates Pólya's formula with cycle counts from computeNumCyclesOfPerm.

The result then follows from \emph{Pólya's enumeration theorem} (Proposition~\ref{prop:numDistinctColorings-eq-sum-card-pow-numCyclesOfGroup-div-mul-card-group}) and the correctness of \emph{computeNumCyclesOfPerm} (Proposition~\ref{prop:computeNumCyclesOfPerm-eq-numCyclesOfPerm}).

nodes.name: Proof of Number of distinct colorings under the trivial group
nodes.statement: We define a bijection $\varphi : Y^X/\{1\} \to Y^X$ by: \begin{equation*} \varphi([f]) = f, \quad \varphi^{-1}(f) = [f]. \end{equation*} This is well-defined since: \begin{equation*} [f] = [h] \implies f = 1 \cdot h = h. \end{equation*} It follows that: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/\{1\}| = |Y^X| = |Y|^{|X|}. \end{equation*} Alternatively, we can derive the result using \emph{Pólya's enumeration theorem}: \begin{equation*} |Y^X/\{1\}| = \frac{1}{|\{1\}|} \sum_{g \in \{1\}} |Y|^{c(g)} = |Y|^{|X|}. \end{equation*} We used the fact that $1$ has $|X|$ cycles.
nodes.statement_short: Bijection between orbits and colorings; alternatively Pólya's theorem with $c(1)=|X|$.

This is defined separately since we do not have a finite group $\mathbb{Z}_0$. This definition is inspired by the fact that $Y^\emptyset$ contains exactly one function.

nodes.name: Cube faces
nodes.statement: We interpret the elements of $[6]$ as $6$ faces of the cube as follows: \begin{itemize} \item $0$ is the face at the front, \item $1$ is the face at the right, \item $2$ is the face at the back, \item $3$ is the face at the left, \item $4$ is the face at the top, \item $5$ is the face at the bottom. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Rotational symmetries of the cube
nodes.statement: We define two fundamental rotations of the cube: \begin{itemize} \item $r = (0\ 1\ 2\ 3)$: A rotation of the cube by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ around the vertical axis passing through the centers of the top and bottom faces. The front face moves to the position of the right face. \item $s = (1\ 4\ 3\ 5)$: A rotation of the cube by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ around the horizontal axis passing through the centers of the front and back faces. The right face moves to the position of the top face. \end{itemize} The set of rotational symmetries of the cube is given by: \begin{equation*} S = \{r^i \cdot s^j \mid i, j \in [4]\} \cup \{s^{2i + 1} \cdot r \cdot s^j \mid i \in [2], j \in [4]\}. \end{equation*} The reasoning is as follows: \begin{itemize} \item First, we apply $s$ at most three times to set the position of face $1$. \item Then, we move face $0$ to any other position using appropriate rotations. To move $0$ to one of the faces in $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, we apply $r$ the necessary number of times. To move $0$ to $4$ or $5$, we first apply $r$ once to move $0$ to $1$, then apply $s$ either once or three times. \end{itemize} Since we can move $0$ to any position and $1$ to any position adjacent to the new position of $0$ (by applying $s$ an appropriate amount of times in the beginning), this results in $6 \times 4 = 24$ distinct rotational symmetries. Because the entire cube configuration is determined by the new positions of faces $0$ and $1$, we have all rotational symmetries of the cube.
nodes.statement_short: Generators $r,s$ of cube rotations and the 24-element set $S$ of all rotational symmetries, with a counting argument.
nodes.label: def:rotationalSymmetriesOfCube

nodes.name: Reduction of exponents modulo the order
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a monoid. If $m \in M$ satisfies $m^n = 1$, then for any $i, j \in [n]$, we have: \begin{equation*} m^{(i + j) \bmod n} = m^{i + j}. \end{equation*}

$m \in M$ satisfies $m^n = 1$
for any $i, j \in [n]$
conclusions: m^{(i + j) \bmod n} = m^{i + j}.

nodes.name: Proof of Reduction of exponents modulo the order
nodes.statement: If $i + j < n$, the result follows immediately. Otherwise, since $n \leq i + j < 2n$, we have: \begin{equation*} m^{i + j} = m^{i + j - n} \cdot m^n = m^{(i + j) \bmod n}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether $i+j<n$.

If also $n = 0$, then $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot x \in S$. \\ All inductive steps are proven in the same manner, using Proposition~\ref{prop:mul_mem_rotationalSymmetriesOfCube} to reduce an exponent by $1$ and applying the inductive hypothesis.

nodes.name: Unordered indistinguishable objects
nodes.statement: We interpret the elements of $[n]$ as $n$ unordered, indistinguishable objects.

nodes.name: Action of S_n on [n]
nodes.statement: The group $S_n$, consisting of all permutations of $[n]$, acts on $[n]$.

nodes.name: Equivalent colorings of unordered objects
nodes.statement: Since we can permute the objects in any way and still get an equivalent configuration, two colorings are equivalent if and only if they color the same number of objects with each color.
assumptions: Since we can permute the objects in any way and still get an equivalent configuration
conclusions: two colorings are equivalent if and only if they color the same number of objects with each color
equivalent_conditions: they color the same number of objects with each color

nodes.name: Number of distinct colorings of unordered objects
nodes.statement: The number of distinct colorings of \emph{$n$ unordered, indistinguishable objects with $m$ colors} is \begin{equation*} |[m]^{[n]}/S_n|. \end{equation*}
nodes.definiendum: number of distinct colorings of $n$ unordered, indistinguishable objects with $m$ colors
nodes.label: def:numDistinctColoringsOfPerm

nodes.name: Number of weak compositions
nodes.statement: The number of weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts is: \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n = m = 0, \\ 0 & \text{if } m = 0 \text{ and } n > 0, \\ \binom{n + m - 1}{m - 1} & \text{if } m > 0. \end{cases} \end{equation*} This is the number of ways to separate $n$ objects into $m$ ordered sets.
nodes.definiendum: number of weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts
nodes.label: def:numWeakCompositions

nodes.name: Contraction and expansion of colorings
nodes.statement: We define functions that contract and expand the domain and codomain of colorings: \begin{itemize} \item \emph{contractCodomain}: Given a coloring $f : [n] \to [m + 1]$ and a proof that $f$ does not map any element to $m$, this function returns $f$ with codomain contracted to $[m]$. \item \emph{expandCodomain}: Given a coloring $f : [n] \to [m]$, this function returns $f$ with codomain expanded to $[m + 1]$. \item \emph{contractDomain}: Given a coloring $f : [n + 1] \to [m]$, this function returns $f$ with domain contracted to $[n]$. \item \emph{expandDomain}: Given a coloring $f : [n] \to [m + 1]$, this function returns $f$ with domain expanded to $[n + 1]$, where $f(n) = m$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:colorings-contract-expand

nodes.name: Image of the preimage of n
nodes.statement: Let $\pi \in S_n$ be such that $\pi(i) = n$ for some $i < n$. Then $\pi(\pi(i)) < n$.
assumptions: Let $\pi \in S_n$ be such that $\pi(i) = n$ for some $i < n$.
conclusions: Then $\pi(\pi(i)) < n$.
nodes.label: prop:perm-perm-val-lt-of-perm-val-eq

nodes.name: Proof of Image of the preimage of n
nodes.statement: Assume, for a contradiction, that $\pi(\pi(i)) \geq n$. Then \begin{equation*} \pi(\pi(i)) = n = \pi(i) \implies \pi(i) = i \implies i = n < n, \end{equation*} which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction from injectivity of $\pi$.

nodes.name: Contraction and expansion of permutations
nodes.statement: We define functions that contract and expand permutations: \begin{itemize} \item \emph{permContract}: Contracts $\pi \in S_{n + 1}$ by removing $n$ from the domain and remapping $\pi^{-1}(n) \mapsto \pi(n)$, if $\pi^{-1}(n) \neq n$. The result is a permutation in $S_n$ whose inverse can be constructed by using the same procedure on $\pi^{-1}$. \item \emph{permExpand}: Expands a permutation $\pi \in S_n$ by adding $n$ to the domain and defining $\pi(n) = n$. The result is a permutation in $S_{n + 1}$, whose inverse can be constructed by using the same procedure on $\pi^{-1}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:perm-contract-expand

nodes.name: Recurrence for colorings of unordered objects
nodes.statement: A recurrence formula for the number of distinct colorings of $n + 1$ unordered, indistinguishable objects with $m + 1$ colors: \begin{equation*} |[m + 1]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}| = |[m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}| + |[m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n|. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Pascal-type recurrence: split by whether the extra colour is used.
nodes.label: prop:numDistinctColoringsOfPerm-succ-succ

nodes.name: Proof of Recurrence for colorings of unordered objects
nodes.statement: We construct a bijection \begin{equation*} \varphi : \left([m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}\right) \cup \left([m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n\right) \to [m + 1]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}. \end{equation*} The function $\varphi$ is defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item For $[f] \in [m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}$, we set \begin{equation*} \varphi([f]) = [\textit{expandCodomain}(f)]. \end{equation*} This is well-defined since if $f_1 = g \cdot f_2$, then \begin{equation*} \textit{expandCodomain}(f_1) = g \cdot (\textit{expandCodomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} \item For $[f] \in [m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n$, we set \begin{equation*} \varphi([f]) = [\textit{expandDomain}(f)]. \end{equation*} This is well-defined since if $f_1 = g \cdot f_2$, then \begin{equation*} \textit{expandDomain}(f_1) = (\textit{permExpand}(g)) \cdot (\textit{expandDomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} \end{itemize} We now prove that $\varphi$ is a bijection. \\ \textbf{Injectivity:} Suppose $\varphi([f_1]) = \varphi([f_2])$. Then either: \begin{itemize} \item no function in $\varphi([f_1]) = \varphi([f_2])$ maps to $m$, which implies \begin{equation*} [f_1], [f_2] \in [m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}. \end{equation*} In this case, we have \begin{equation*} [\textit{expandCodomain}(f_1)] = [\textit{expandCodomain}(f_2)] \end{equation*} so \begin{equation*} \textit{expandCodomain}(f_1) = g \cdot (\textit{expandCodomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} This implies $f_1 = g \cdot f_2$, so $[f_1] = [f_2]$. \item some function in $\varphi([f_1]) = \varphi([f_2])$ maps to $m$, which implies \begin{equation*} [f_1], [f_2] \in [m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n. \end{equation*} In this case, we have \begin{equation*} [\textit{expandDomain}(f_1)] = [\textit{expandDomain}(f_2)], \end{equation*} so \begin{equation*} \textit{expandDomain}(f_1) = g \cdot (\textit{expandDomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} This implies that \begin{equation*} f_1(x) = ((\textit{permContract}(g)) \cdot f_2)(x) \end{equation*} for all $x \in [n] \setminus \{g \cdot n\}$. \\ If $g \cdot n \neq n$, then we have \begin{align*} f_1(g \cdot n) &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_1)(g \cdot n) \\ &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_2)(n) \\ &= m \\ &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_1)(n) \\ &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_2)(g^{-1} \cdot n) \\ &= f_2(g^{-1} \cdot n) \\ &= ((\textit{permContract}(g)) \cdot f_2)(g \cdot n). \end{align*} Thus, $[f_1] = [f_2]$. \end{itemize} \textbf{Surjectivity:} Take any $[f] \in [m + 1]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}$. If $f$ does not map any element to $m$, then \begin{equation*} \varphi([\textit{contractCodomain}(f)]) = [f]. \end{equation*} Otherwise, there exists some $i$ such that $f(i) = m$. Define \begin{equation*} h = (i\ n) \cdot f, \end{equation*} where $(i\ n)$ is the transposition swapping $i$ and $n$. Since $h(n) = m$, we have \begin{equation*} \varphi([\textit{contractDomain}(h)]) = [h] = [f]. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Construct an explicit bijection from the disjoint union by expanding codomain or domain, then prove injectivity and surjectivity. Injectivity in the second case uses permContract.

nodes.name: Declare the bijection $\varphi$
nodes.statement: We construct a bijection \begin{equation*} \varphi : \left([m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}\right) \cup \left([m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n\right) \to [m + 1]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Declare the bijection $\varphi$

nodes.name: Define $\varphi$ by expandCodomain / expandDomain and check
nodes.statement: The function $\varphi$ is defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item For $[f] \in [m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}$, we set \begin{equation*} \varphi([f]) = [\textit{expandCodomain}(f)]. \end{equation*} This is well-defined since if $f_1 = g \cdot f_2$, then \begin{equation*} \textit{expandCodomain}(f_1) = g \cdot (\textit{expandCodomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} \item For $[f] \in [m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n$, we set \begin{equation*} \varphi([f]) = [\textit{expandDomain}(f)]. \end{equation*} This is well-defined since if $f_1 = g \cdot f_2$, then \begin{equation*} \textit{expandDomain}(f_1) = (\textit{permExpand}(g)) \cdot (\textit{expandDomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi$ by expandCodomain / expandDomain and check well-definedness

nodes.name: Prove $\varphi$ is bijective
nodes.statement: We now prove that $\varphi$ is a bijection. \\ \textbf{Injectivity:} Suppose $\varphi([f_1]) = \varphi([f_2])$. Then either: \begin{itemize} \item no function in $\varphi([f_1]) = \varphi([f_2])$ maps to $m$, which implies \begin{equation*} [f_1], [f_2] \in [m]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}. \end{equation*} In this case, we have \begin{equation*} [\textit{expandCodomain}(f_1)] = [\textit{expandCodomain}(f_2)] \end{equation*} so \begin{equation*} \textit{expandCodomain}(f_1) = g \cdot (\textit{expandCodomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} This implies $f_1 = g \cdot f_2$, so $[f_1] = [f_2]$. \item some function in $\varphi([f_1]) = \varphi([f_2])$ maps to $m$, which implies \begin{equation*} [f_1], [f_2] \in [m + 1]^{[n]}/S_n. \end{equation*} In this case, we have \begin{equation*} [\textit{expandDomain}(f_1)] = [\textit{expandDomain}(f_2)], \end{equation*} so \begin{equation*} \textit{expandDomain}(f_1) = g \cdot (\textit{expandDomain}(f_2)). \end{equation*} This implies that \begin{equation*} f_1(x) = ((\textit{permContract}(g)) \cdot f_2)(x) \end{equation*} for all $x \in [n] \setminus \{g \cdot n\}$. \\ If $g \cdot n \neq n$, then we have \begin{align*} f_1(g \cdot n) &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_1)(g \cdot n) \\ &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_2)(n) \\ &= m \\ &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_1)(n) \\ &= \textit{expandDomain}(f_2)(g^{-1} \cdot n) \\ &= f_2(g^{-1} \cdot n) \\ &= ((\textit{permContract}(g)) \cdot f_2)(g \cdot n). \end{align*} Thus, $[f_1] = [f_2]$. \end{itemize} \textbf{Surjectivity:} Take any $[f] \in [m + 1]^{[n + 1]}/S_{n + 1}$. If $f$ does not map any element to $m$, then \begin{equation*} \varphi([\textit{contractCodomain}(f)]) = [f]. \end{equation*} Otherwise, there exists some $i$ such that $f(i) = m$. Define \begin{equation*} h = (i\ n) \cdot f, \end{equation*} where $(i\ n)$ is the transposition swapping $i$ and $n$. Since $h(n) = m$, we have \begin{equation*} \varphi([\textit{contractDomain}(h)]) = [h] = [f]. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Colorings of unordered objects are counted by weak compositions
nodes.statement: The number of distinct colorings of $n$ unordered, indistinguishable objects with $m$ colors is equal to the number of weak compositions of $n$ with $m$ parts.
also_stated_at: Thus, the number of distinct colorings of $n$ unordered, indistinguishable objects with $m$ colors is equal to the number of ways to separate $n$ objects into $m$ ordered sets (i.e., the number of weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts).
We now prove that the number of distinct colorings of $n$ unordered, indistinguishable objects with $m$ colors is equal to the number of weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts.
nodes.statement_short: $|[m]^{[n]}/S_n|$ equals the number of weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts.
nodes.label: prop:numDistinctColoringsOfPerm-eq-numWeakCompositions

nodes.name: Proof of Colorings of unordered objects are counted by weak compositions
nodes.statement: We use induction on $m + n$. \\ If $m + n = 0$, then $n = m = 0$, and we have $|\emptyset^\emptyset / S_0| = 1$. \\ Otherwise we first check cases when $n = 0$ or $m = 0$ and see that the result holds. \\ If $n > 0$ and $m > 0$, applying Proposition~\ref{prop:numDistinctColoringsOfPerm-succ-succ} and the inductive hypothesis, we obtain \begin{equation*} |[m]^{[n]}/S_n| = |[m - 1]^{[n]}/S_n| + |[m]^{[n - 1]}/S_n| = \binom{n + m - 2}{m - 2} + \binom{n + m - 2}{m - 1} = \binom{n + m - 1}{m - 1}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Stirling numbers of the first kind
nodes.statement: The \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_numbers_of_the_first_kind}{\texttt{Stirling numbers of the first kind}} count the number of permutations of a set of size $n$ with exactly $k$ cycles: \begin{equation*} s(n, k) = |\{\pi \in S_n \mid c(\pi) = k\}|, \end{equation*} where $c(\pi)$ denotes the number of cycles in the permutation $\pi$.

nodes.name: Sum of Stirling numbers of the first kind
nodes.statement: For any $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m > 0$, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{k = 0}^n s(n, k) m^k = n! \binom{n + m - 1}{m - 1}. \end{equation*} Additionally: \begin{itemize} \item If $n = m = 0$, the sum evaluates to $1$ in Lean, since $0^0 = 1$. \item If $n > 0$ and $m = 0$, the sum evaluates to $0$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Proof of Sum of Stirling numbers of the first kind
nodes.statement: We apply \emph{Pólya's enumeration theorem} (Proposition~\ref{prop:numDistinctColorings-mul-card-group-eq-sum-numGroupOfNumCycles-mul-card-pow}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:numDistinctColoringsOfPerm-eq-numWeakCompositions}: \begin{equation*} \sum_{k = 0}^n s(n, k) m^k = |[m]^{[n]}/S_n| \cdot |S_n| = n! \binom{n + m - 1}{m - 1}. \end{equation*}
